Migrate SQL Server (VM) to Azure SQL Database Using BACPAC

Nithin Sunke · October 31, 2026 · 12 min read

A hands-on offline migration of a 16.8-million-row banking database from SQL Server on a VM to a free-tier Azure SQL Database, using SqlPackage export and import, with every step validated.

In this post

  2. Lab environment
  3. Install SqlPackage

  5. Stop writes on the source
  6. Export the BACPAC
  7. Prepare the target
  8. Import into Azure SQL Database

  11. Issues I hit and fixes
  12. Results and takeaways

How BACPAC migration works

A BACPAC is a zip file containing a database's schema and data. SqlPackage exports it from SQL Server and imports it into Azure SQL Database. Coming from Oracle, think of it as expdp/impdp rather than RMAN: it is a logical copy, not a physical backup.

SQL Server (VM) ──SqlPackage Export──▶ scsbank.bacpac ──SqlPackage Import──▶ Azure SQL Database

It's an offline method: the application must stop writing while the export runs, so downtime ≈ export time + import time. That makes it ideal for small to medium databases and labs. For large databases or near-zero downtime, use transactional replication instead.

Lab environment

ComponentDetails
SourceSQL Server on a Windows VM (mssqlsrv01), database scsbank
TargetAzure SQL logical server cisql01 (Central India), database scsbank, Free offer – General Purpose Serverless, Gen5, 2 vCores
Data17 tables across 10 schemas, about 16.8 million rows
ToolsSqlPackage 170.4.83.3 on the VM; VS Code with the mssql extension for queries

Install SqlPackage

The dotnet tool install route needs the .NET SDK, which wasn't on the VM. The standalone zip has everything built in, so I used that:

# Download and extract
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://aka.ms/sqlpackage-windows" -OutFile "$env:TEMP\sqlpackage.zip"
Expand-Archive -Path "$env:TEMP\sqlpackage.zip" -DestinationPath "C:\sqlpackage" -Force

# Add to PATH (current session + permanently)
$env:Path += ";C:\sqlpackage"
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","Machine") + ";C:\sqlpackage", "Machine")

sqlpackage /version     # 170.4.83.3

Assess the source database

Azure SQL Database doesn't support some SQL Server features, and the export fails validation on them. Check these before exporting.

1Check database size

USE scsbank;
EXEC sp_spaceused;

2Record row counts

Save these; you'll compare them with the target after the import.

SELECT s.name AS schema_name, t.name AS table_name, SUM(p.rows) AS row_count
FROM sys.tables t
JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id = s.schema_id
JOIN sys.partitions p ON t.object_id = p.object_id AND p.index_id IN (0,1)
GROUP BY s.name, t.name
ORDER BY 1, 2;

3Check for cross-database references

Each Azure SQL Database is isolated, so three-part names such as OtherDB.dbo.Table aren't supported.

SELECT OBJECT_SCHEMA_NAME(d.referencing_id) AS schema_name,
       OBJECT_NAME(d.referencing_id)        AS object_name,
       o.type_desc,
       d.referenced_database_name,
       d.referenced_schema_name,
       d.referenced_entity_name
FROM sys.sql_expression_dependencies d
JOIN sys.objects o ON o.object_id = d.referencing_id
WHERE d.referenced_database_name IS NOT NULL
  AND d.referenced_database_name <> DB_NAME();

4Check for synonyms pointing to other databases

SELECT name, base_object_name FROM sys.synonyms;
If you do find cross-database references: merge the databases into one (move the other tables into their own schema), migrate both and use Elastic Query external tables (read-only), move the logic into the application, or drop unused objects. The export won't succeed until they're gone.

5Check for Windows-authenticated users

SELECT name, type_desc FROM sys.database_principals
WHERE type IN ('U','G');

dbo appears as a Windows user only because a Windows account owns the database. BACPAC skips dbo, so this doesn't block the export, but changing the owner to sa is good practice:

USE master;
ALTER AUTHORIZATION ON DATABASE::scsbank TO sa;

USE scsbank;
SELECT name, type_desc FROM sys.database_principals WHERE name = 'dbo';

Any other Windows users (e.g. DOMAIN\appuser) must be dropped before export and recreated in Azure as contained users.

Stop writes on the source

For a transactionally consistent export, nothing may change while it runs. Putting the database in read-only mode is the simplest way:

ALTER DATABASE scsbank SET READ_ONLY WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE;

Export the BACPAC

Run on the source VM. Write the file to a drive with free space of 1–3× the database size.

SqlPackage /Action:Export `
  /SourceServerName:localhost `
  /SourceDatabaseName:scsbank `
  /SourceTrustServerCertificate:True `
  /TargetFile:"B:\export\scsbank.bacpac" `
  /p:VerifyFullTextDocumentTypesSupported=False
In PowerShell, use a backtick ` to continue a line. The ^ character only works in Command Prompt. Or keep the whole command on one line.

Once the export finishes, put the source back to read-write. This is also your rollback if the migration needs to be abandoned:

ALTER DATABASE scsbank SET READ_WRITE;

Prepare the target

Important for the free offer: if SqlPackage creates the database itself, it creates a paid database. To stay free, first create an empty database with SQL database (Free offer) in the portal, then import into it. The target must be empty: no user tables.

Then check the logical server:

  • Firewall: under SQL server → Security → Networking, allow the public IP of the VM running SqlPackage.
  • Authentication: make sure SQL authentication is enabled (not Entra-only) and you know the server admin password.
  • Network: the VM needs outbound TCP 1433 to <server>.database.windows.net.

Before importing, confirm the login works from the VM:

$cs = "Server=tcp:cisql01.database.windows.net,1433;Database=scsbank;User ID=nsunke;Password=<password>;Encrypt=True;"
$c = New-Object System.Data.SqlClient.SqlConnection $cs; $c.Open(); "Connected: " + $c.State; $c.Close()

Import into Azure SQL Database

SqlPackage /Action:Import `
  /SourceFile:"B:\export\scsbank.bacpac" `
  /TargetServerName:cisql01.database.windows.net `
  /TargetDatabaseName:scsbank `
  /TargetUser:nsunke /TargetPassword:'<password>' `
  /TargetEncryptConnection:True

Three yellow warnings appeared during the import. None of them are errors:

  • "A project which specifies SQL Server 2025 … may experience compatibility issues": the BACPAC records the source version. It's informational; the import validates the schema against Azure SQL.
  • "The object [data_0] / [log] exists in the target, but it will not be dropped": these are the empty target database's own file objects. They're expected when importing into a pre-created database.

Validate

Run the same queries on the target and compare with the source:

-- Row counts
SELECT s.name, t.name, SUM(p.rows) AS row_count
FROM sys.tables t
JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id = s.schema_id
JOIN sys.partitions p ON t.object_id = p.object_id AND p.index_id IN (0,1)
GROUP BY s.name, t.name ORDER BY 1,2;

-- Object counts by type (run on both sides)
SELECT type_desc, COUNT(*) FROM sys.objects
WHERE is_ms_shipped = 0 GROUP BY type_desc ORDER BY 1;

Post-migration tasks

-- Application user (contained user, no server login needed)
CREATE USER appuser WITH PASSWORD = '<StrongPassword>';
ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER appuser;
ALTER ROLE db_datawriter ADD MEMBER appuser;

-- Refresh statistics after the bulk load
EXEC sp_updatestats;
  • Not migrated by BACPAC: server logins, SQL Agent jobs and linked servers. Recreate logins as contained users; move jobs to Elastic Jobs or Azure Automation.
  • Connection string: Server=tcp:cisql01.database.windows.net,1433;Database=scsbank;Encrypt=True;
  • Free offer: disconnect tools when you're done. Open connections stop the database from auto-pausing and use up the free vCore seconds.

Issues I hit and fixes

IssueCauseFix
sqlpackage / dotnet not recognized.NET SDK not installedUse the standalone SqlPackage zip and add C:\sqlpackage to PATH
Free database creation failedFree offer isn't available in every region (e.g. India South Central)Create the server in a supported region; Central India worked
Login failed for user 'nsunke'Wrong admin password for the new server. The firewall was fine; a firewall block reports "Client with IP address … is not allowed"Reset the password on the server's Overview page, test the login, then rerun the import
dbo listed as WINDOWS_USERDatabase owned by a Windows accountALTER AUTHORIZATION ON DATABASE::scsbank TO sa

Results and takeaways

MetricValue
Rows migrated16,760,354 across 17 tables
Export time1 min 2 s
Import time12 min 1 s (free tier, 2 vCores)
Downtime (writes blocked)Export duration only in this lab; in production it's export + import + cutover
Data validation100% row-count match
  • Assessment queries take two minutes and prevent most export failures. Run them first.
  • Import is the slow part, and it scales with the target's compute. For production, import into a larger tier and scale down afterwards.
  • Pre-create the database when you want the free offer; otherwise SqlPackage creates a paid one.
  • Wrap passwords in single quotes in PowerShell, and keep them out of screenshots.
  • For databases beyond about 100–150 GB, or when downtime must be minutes, use transactional replication instead.
